A Low-Incidence Vaccine Efficacy Example

Source: vignettes/Example.Rmd
Example.Rmd
library(poissonexact)

Why this vignette exists

The companion vignette, vignette("Theory-Implementation"), derives why exact conditional inference works and how each of this package’s three algorithms computes it. This vignette is the “so what”: a single, realistic scenario where the difference between exact inference and the usual asymptotic (Wald) approach is not academic.

Vaccine efficacy trials are close to the worst case for large-sample approximations, for exactly the reasons vignette("Theory-Implementation") Section 1 lists: the outcome (a confirmed case) is rare, the trial is often broken into several strata (age band, region, risk group) each with only a handful of events, and a genuinely effective vaccine pushes the observed rate ratio toward the edge of what a handful of events can distinguish from zero. That is precisely the regime this package targets.

This vignette does three things:

  1. Simulates a small, stratified, low-incidence vaccine efficacy trial.
  2. Analyses it with ep_closed_form() and, for comparison, with glm()’s ordinary asymptotic (Wald) inference, fit to the same model, using the equivalence between stratifying and adjusting for a fully saturated factor established in vignette("Theory-Implementation") Section 4.1-4.2.
  3. Shows how an already-computed exact distribution can be reused to answer a different question (a different null hypothesis, or a different confidence level) without repeating the combinatorial work that built it in the first place (vignette("Theory-Implementation") Sections 6.5 and 8.4).

A small Monte Carlo study at the end repeats the simulation many times to check, empirically, how often each method’s nominal 95% interval actually contains the true value, rather than relying on a single lucky (or unlucky) draw to make the point.

The scenario

Consider a trial with two arms (vaccine, placebo), each followed for one year, stratified into three age bands with different baseline attack rates: older participants are assumed to be at higher baseline risk of the outcome. The vaccine is assumed to reduce the incidence rate by the same proportion in every stratum: a true vaccine efficacy of 70% (a true rate ratio of 0.30), exactly the “constant across strata” assumption that every algorithm in this package makes for the effect under test (vignette("Theory-Implementation") Section 2.4).

This trial is deliberately sized small, a few hundred participants per stratum rather than a few thousand, because the point of this vignette is sharpest exactly where events are scarce. As the next section shows, a trial this size can (and, with the seed fixed below, does) come back with zero observed vaccine-arm cases in every single stratum by chance alone, even though the vaccine is genuinely 70% effective. That outcome is not a contrived pathology; it is a realistic, if unlucky, draw from a small low-incidence trial, and it is exactly the situation where the choice of analysis method matters most.

age_grp <- factor(
  c("18-40", "41-64", "65+"),
  levels = c("18-40", "41-64", "65+")
)

true_ve <- 0.70 # true vaccine efficacy, constant across strata
true_rr <- 1 - true_ve # true rate ratio, vaccine vs. placebo
true_beta <- log(true_rr) # true log rate ratio (the target of inference)

trial_design <- data.frame(
  age_grp = rep(age_grp, each = 2),
  arm = factor(
    rep(c("placebo", "vaccine"), times = 3),
    levels = c("placebo", "vaccine")
  ),
  n = c(300, 300, 250, 250, 150, 150),
  person_years = c(300, 300, 250, 250, 150, 150),
  placebo_rate = rep(c(0.0060, 0.0100, 0.0180), each = 2)
)
trial_design$true_rate <- with(
  trial_design,
  ifelse(
    arm == "vaccine",
    placebo_rate * true_rr,
    placebo_rate
  )
)
trial_design$expected_cases <- with(trial_design, person_years * true_rate)
trial_design
#>   age_grp     arm   n person_years placebo_rate true_rate expected_cases
#> 1   18-40 placebo 300          300        0.006    0.0060           1.80
#> 2   18-40 vaccine 300          300        0.006    0.0018           0.54
#> 3   41-64 placebo 250          250        0.010    0.0100           2.50
#> 4   41-64 vaccine 250          250        0.010    0.0030           0.75
#> 5     65+ placebo 150          150        0.018    0.0180           2.70
#> 6     65+ vaccine 150          150        0.018    0.0054           0.81

Even before simulating anything, notice how small the expected case counts already are, especially in the vaccine arm: under 1 expected case in every single stratum (0.54, 0.75, and 0.81), and under 3 even in the larger placebo arm. This is the sparse-data regime vignette("Theory-Implementation") Section 1 motivates specifically so that the vaccine arm’s expected counts sit close enough to zero that an all-zero outcome is a real, non-negligible possibility rather than a one-in-a-million curiosity.

Simulating the trial

Actual case counts are simulated from these expected values with a fixed seed, so this document reproduces identically every time it is rendered.

set.seed(2026)
trial_design$cases <- rpois(nrow(trial_design), trial_design$expected_cases)
trial_design[, c(
  "age_grp",
  "arm",
  "n",
  "person_years",
  "expected_cases",
  "cases"
)]
#>   age_grp     arm   n person_years expected_cases cases
#> 1   18-40 placebo 300          300           1.80     2
#> 2   18-40 vaccine 300          300           0.54     0
#> 3   41-64 placebo 250          250           2.50     1
#> 4   41-64 vaccine 250          250           0.75     0
#> 5     65+ placebo 150          150           2.70     3
#> 6     65+ vaccine 150          150           0.81     0

With expected counts this low, it would not be at all unusual for one or more cells above to come out as 0, 1, or 2 cases by chance alone. With the seed fixed above, that is exactly what happened here: every vaccine-arm cell came back with zero observed cases, while the placebo arm shows a handful of events in every stratum. A vaccine-arm total of zero is not a data error and not a sign the simulation is broken; with expected vaccine-arm counts of 0.54, 0.75, and 0.81 (summing to a total expected count of only 2.1), an all-zero outcome across all three strata has roughly a 1-in-8 chance of happening on any given trial (e^{-2.1} \approx 0.12), purely from Poisson variation, even though the vaccine is genuinely working. This is precisely where asymptotic Wald inference is at its least trustworthy, and precisely where exact conditional inference has no such weakness, because it never relies on a large-sample approximation in the first place. The next two sections show what each method actually does with this data.

Recommended: aggregate repeated covariate patterns before fitting

Every algorithm in this package (ep_closed_form(), ep_multi_shift(), ep_network()) processes its input one row at a time when building the exact conditional distribution. If your raw data has multiple rows that share the exact same covariate pattern (every column that enters the model, plus strata, plus (if used) the EXACTMAX variable), summing those rows into one before fitting is a free performance win, not an approximation: it never changes the exact result.

The reason this is exact, not just a convenient shortcut, is the same sufficiency argument the algorithms themselves are built on (vignette("Theory-Implementation")): independent Poisson counts that share the same rate parameter sum to a Poisson with the combined exposure (the standard Poisson convolution identity). Concretely, if two rows are identical on every column the model conditions on and differ only in their own cases/exposure, replacing them with one row (cases summed, exposure summed, or, if offset_log = TRUE, the log-offset combined as log(sum(exp(log_offset)))) gives the identical sufficient statistics the dynamic program would have derived from the two original rows. This matters in practice because the dynamic program’s cost grows with the number of rows processed, not the number of underlying subjects; collapsing, say, patient-level records down to one row per distinct covariate pattern can turn a slow fit into an instant one with no change to any p-value or confidence interval.

One caveat: this equivalence is only exactly guaranteed under two of the package’s three SAS-style per-observation cap rules: EXACTMAX = var (as long as every merged row shares the same EXACTMAX value) and the no-offset/no-EXACTMAX default (whose cap is always the whole stratum total regardless of how many rows it’s split across). Under the third rule (offset supplied without EXACTMAX, where each row’s own cap is derived from its own exposure), pre-aggregating changes which computational truncation bound gets enumerated against, since that per-row cap doesn’t combine linearly under merging. In practice this essentially never changes the answer (the cap is a generous bound the true distribution almost never approaches), but it isn’t on the same provably-exact footing as the other two rules; if that distinction matters for a particular analysis, verify by comparing the aggregated and unaggregated fits directly, as below.

The example below is one row per age_grp x arm cell already (the smallest this data naturally gets), so there is nothing left to aggregate in trial_design itself. To make the point concretely, this recreates the same trial as if it had instead arrived as separate per-site records: three recruiting sites contributing to every cell, each with its own slice of that cell’s person-years and (simulated) cases, and confirms that aggregating back down to one row per cell before fitting gives an identical result to fitting the per-site data directly:

set.seed(20260819)
n_sites <- 3

# Same 6 cells as trial_design, but split into 3 site-level rows each,
# with person_years randomly divided across sites (summing back to the
# original cell total) and cases simulated per site.
trial_design_by_site <- do.call(
  rbind, lapply(seq_len(nrow(trial_design)), function(i) {
  cell <- trial_design[i, ]
  py_split <- as.numeric(
    rmultinom(1, cell$person_years, prob = rep(1, n_sites)))
  data.frame(
    age_grp = cell$age_grp,
    arm = cell$arm,
    site = paste0("site", seq_len(n_sites)),
    person_years = py_split,
    cases = rpois(n_sites, py_split * cell$placebo_rate *
      ifelse(cell$arm == "vaccine", true_rr, 1))
  )
}))
trial_design_by_site <-
  trial_design_by_site[trial_design_by_site$person_years > 0, ]
nrow(trial_design_by_site)
#> [1] 18

# Aggregate back down to one row per (age_grp, arm) pattern: sum cases and
# person_years within each group (no log() needed here, since this
# vignette's offset_log = FALSE throughout; person_years is already the
# raw exposure).
trial_design_agg <- aggregate(
  cbind(cases, person_years) ~ age_grp + arm,
  data = trial_design_by_site,
  FUN = sum
)

fit_by_site <- ep_closed_form(
  formula = cases ~ arm,
  data = trial_design_by_site,
  offset = "person_years",
  offset_log = FALSE,
  strata = "age_grp",
  ref_levels = list(arm = "placebo"),
  verbose = FALSE
)

fit_agg <- ep_closed_form(
  formula = cases ~ arm,
  data = trial_design_agg,
  offset = "person_years",
  offset_log = FALSE,
  strata = "age_grp",
  ref_levels = list(arm = "placebo"),
  verbose = FALSE
)

# Identical estimate, CI, and p-value either way; aggregating first only
# changed how many rows the dynamic program had to process, not the answer.
all.equal(
  fit_by_site$exactparmest[, c("Estimate", "LowerCL", "UpperCL", "PValue")],
  fit_agg$exactparmest[, c("Estimate", "LowerCL", "UpperCL", "PValue")]
)
#> [1] TRUE

This particular demonstration uses ep_closed_form(), which has no per-observation cap of any kind (see ?ep_closed_form’s Details), so aggregation is exact here unconditionally, independent of the Rule 3 caveat above. ep_multi_shift() and ep_network() follow the same convolution argument for the same reason, but do go through the EXACTMAX/offset cap rules described above; the caveat there only bites when offset is supplied without EXACTMAX, and even then only in the rare case where that heuristic cap is actually close to binding.

The rest of this vignette continues to use trial_design as originally simulated (already one row per cell); the recommendation is simply to do the equivalent of the aggregate() step above on your own raw data before calling any of this package’s fitting functions, whenever your data has more rows than distinct covariate patterns.

Analysing it the exact way

ep_closed_form() is the right tool here: one two-level effect of interest (arm), with age strata as the only other structure in the model (vignette("Theory-Implementation") Section 6.1).

fit_exact <- ep_closed_form(
  formula = cases ~ arm,
  data = trial_design,
  offset = "person_years",
  offset_log = FALSE,
  strata = "age_grp",
  ref_levels = list(arm = "placebo"),
  verbose = FALSE
)
fit_exact
#> 
#> Exact conditional Poisson, two groups + strata (closed-form Guess & Thomas algorithm)
#> -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
#>   Parameter Estimate StdError Alpha LowerCL    UpperCL  PValue SuffStat
#>  armvaccine     -Inf       NA  0.05    -Inf -0.1633296 0.03125        0

The observed vaccine-arm total (SuffStat) sits at 0, the very edge of what this statistic can attain, since it cannot go any lower. vignette("Theory-Implementation") Sections 8.3-8.4 describe exactly this situation: when the observed value is at the boundary of its attainable range, the corresponding confidence limit is set to \mp\infty directly rather than estimated, and here that shows up as Estimate = -Inf and LowerCL = -Inf. This is not a failure or a placeholder; it is the exact, honest answer to “how small could the true rate ratio be and still be consistent with zero observed events?”: arbitrarily small, so the interval says so explicitly instead of printing a number that looks precise but isn’t. The upper limit and the p-value are still perfectly well defined and informative, as the next chunk shows.

Estimate is on the \beta = \log(\text{rate ratio}) scale used throughout vignette("Theory-Implementation"). Converting to the rate-ratio and vaccine-efficacy scales:

rr_exact <- exp(fit_exact$exactparmest$Estimate)
rr_ci_exact <- exp(c(
  fit_exact$exactparmest$LowerCL,
  fit_exact$exactparmest$UpperCL
))

ve_exact <- 1 - rr_exact
ve_ci_exact <- rev(1 - rr_ci_exact)

cat(sprintf(
  paste("Exact:  RR = %.3f (95%% CI %.3f, %.3f)",
  "   VE = %.1f%% (95%% CI %.1f%%, %.1f%%)   p = %.4f\n"),
  rr_exact,
  rr_ci_exact[1],
  rr_ci_exact[2],
  100 * ve_exact,
  100 * ve_ci_exact[1],
  100 * ve_ci_exact[2],
  fit_exact$exactparmest$PValue
))
#> Exact:  RR = 0.000 (95% CI 0.000, 0.849)    VE = 100.0% (95% CI 15.1%, 100.0%)   p = 0.0312

Analysing the same model with glm()

For a fair comparison, glm() needs to fit the identical model. Age strata, here, are a single categorical variable with nothing else in the model, so vignette("Theory-Implementation") Section 4.1-4.2 guarantees that adjusting for the full set of age_grp dummy columns is an exact reparametrisation of stratifying by age_grp: the same model, just written the ordinary glm() way instead of the strata= way.

fit_glm <- glm(
  cases ~ arm + age_grp + offset(log(person_years)),
  family = poisson(link = "log"),
  data = trial_design
)
summary(fit_glm)$coefficients
#>                 Estimate   Std. Error       z value     Pr(>|z|)
#> (Intercept)   -5.0106353 7.071068e-01 -7.0861083893 1.379358e-12
#> armvaccine   -23.9108390 3.854339e+04 -0.0006203617 9.995050e-01
#> age_grp41-64  -0.5108256 1.224745e+00 -0.4170873753 6.766145e-01
#> age_grp65+     1.0986123 9.128709e-01  1.2034694650 2.287947e-01

Look closely at the armvaccine row: the standard error is four orders of magnitude larger than the estimate itself (\mathrm{SE} \approx 38{,}543 against an estimate of \approx -23.9). That imbalance is the signature of quasi-complete separation: with zero observed events in every vaccine-arm cell, the log-linear model wants to push the vaccine coefficient to -\infty, and the optimizer stops only because it ran out of room to keep moving in a fixed number of iterations, not because it found a well-determined answer. This is exactly the failure mode this section set out to demonstrate, and the next chunk checks for the diagnostic a user would normally rely on to catch it:

cat("fit_glm$converged:", fit_glm$converged, "\n")
#> fit_glm$converged: TRUE

withCallingHandlers(
  glm(
    cases ~ arm + age_grp + offset(log(person_years)),
    family = poisson(link = "log"),
    data = trial_design
  ),
  warning = function(w) cat("Warning raised:", conditionMessage(w), "\n")
)
#> 
#> Call:  glm(formula = cases ~ arm + age_grp + offset(log(person_years)), 
#>     family = poisson(link = "log"), data = trial_design)
#> 
#> Coefficients:
#>  (Intercept)    armvaccine  age_grp41-64    age_grp65+  
#>      -5.0106      -23.9108       -0.5108        1.0986  
#> 
#> Degrees of Freedom: 5 Total (i.e. Null);  2 Residual
#> Null Deviance:       10.87 
#> Residual Deviance: 4.953e-10     AIC: 15.61
cat("(if no \"Warning raised\" line appears above, glm() raised none)\n")
#> (if no "Warning raised" line appears above, glm() raised none)

fit_glm$converged reports TRUE, and glm() raises no warning at all for this fit. There is no glm.fit: fitted rates numerically 0 occurred message, no algorithm did not converge message, nothing: by every signal glm() itself exposes, this fit looks completely unremarkable. A user who checks for warnings before trusting a model, a common and generally reasonable habit, would see nothing here and proceed with unwarranted confidence. The next two chunks show what that unwarranted confidence would actually produce.

The Wald confidence interval and p-value, the usual large-sample approximation vignette("Theory-Implementation") Section 1 warns about, are computed directly from the estimate and its asymptotic standard error, exactly the textbook construction (this uses the plain Wald interval, not a profile-likelihood interval, to isolate the specific approximation being compared against):

co_glm <- summary(fit_glm)$coefficients["armvaccine", ]
z975 <- qnorm(0.975)

beta_glm <- co_glm["Estimate"]
wald_ci_beta <- beta_glm + c(-1, 1) * z975 * co_glm["Std. Error"]
pval_glm <- co_glm["Pr(>|z|)"]

rr_glm <- exp(beta_glm)
rr_ci_glm <- exp(wald_ci_beta)
ve_glm <- 1 - rr_glm
ve_ci_glm <- rev(1 - rr_ci_glm)

cat(sprintf(
  paste("Wald:   RR = %.3f (95%% CI %.3f, %.3f)",
  "   VE = %.1f%% (95%% CI %.1f%%, %.1f%%)   p = %.4f\n"),
  rr_glm,
  rr_ci_glm[1],
  rr_ci_glm[2],
  100 * ve_glm,
  100 * ve_ci_glm[1],
  100 * ve_ci_glm[2],
  pval_glm
))
#> Wald:   RR = 0.000 (95% CI 0.000, Inf)    VE = 100.0% (95% CI -Inf%, 100.0%)   p = 0.9995

Side by side 

comparison <- data.frame(
  Method = c("Exact (ep_closed_form)", "Wald (glm)"),
  RR = c(rr_exact, rr_glm),
  RR_lo = c(rr_ci_exact[1], rr_ci_glm[1]),
  RR_hi = c(rr_ci_exact[2], rr_ci_glm[2]),
  `VE %` = 100 * c(ve_exact, ve_glm),
  `VE % lo` = 100 * c(ve_ci_exact[1], ve_ci_glm[1]),
  `VE % hi` = 100 * c(ve_ci_exact[2], ve_ci_glm[2]),
  PValue = c(fit_exact$exactparmest$PValue, pval_glm),
  check.names = FALSE
)
knitr::kable(comparison, digits = 4)
Method RR RR_lo RR_hi VE % VE % lo VE % hi PValue
Exact (ep_closed_form) 0 0 0.8493 100 15.0689 100 0.0312
Estimate Wald (glm) 0 0 Inf 100 -Inf 100 0.9995

The two point estimates land in the same place: both report essentially 100% efficacy, since both are estimating the same quantity from the same all-zero vaccine-arm data. If a reader only glanced at the point estimates, this would look like two methods agreeing closely. The two rows tell completely different stories the moment you look past the point estimate:

  • The exact interval, (0.000, 0.849) on the rate-ratio scale, (15.1%, 100.0%) on the efficacy scale, is wide on one side (as it should be, given zero events) but still genuinely informative: it rules out rate ratios above 0.849, i.e., efficacy below 15%, at the 95% level, and its p-value of 0.0312 correctly flags this as a significant result.
  • The Wald interval is (0.000, Inf) on the rate-ratio scale and (-Inf%, 100.0%) on the efficacy scale: literally the entire range of values either quantity could ever take. It rules out nothing. Its p-value, 0.9995, says the opposite of the exact method’s conclusion: no evidence of any effect at all. And, as the previous section showed, glm() reached this completely uninformative, wrong-direction answer while reporting converged = TRUE and raising no warning whatsoever.

This is the central point of this example: a confidence interval spanning every value a parameter could possibly take is every bit as much a sign of a broken fit as an error message would be, but nothing about glm()’s own output says so. Checking summary(fit_glm) for a plausible-looking table of coefficients, or checking warnings() for a diagnostic message, both miss it. The width of the interval itself, and the sheer size of the standard error relative to the estimate, are the only signals available, and they are signals a user has to know to look for. The exact interval never has this problem, not because it happens to give a narrower answer here, but because its width is determined entirely by what the data can and cannot rule out, with no large-sample approximation to silently break down in the first place. Rerunning the simulation chunk above with a different seed will sometimes produce a nonzero (if still small) vaccine-arm count, in which case both methods will report finite, comparable intervals; this is exactly the comparison the Monte Carlo study at the end of this vignette runs systematically, rather than leaving it to one draw of the dice.

Cross-checking with the general algorithms

vignette("Theory-Implementation") Section 4.1-4.2 is not just a theoretical curiosity here; it is directly checkable. Adjusting for age_grp as an ordinary covariate (instead of stratifying by it) should give exactly the same exact inference, because age is the only nuisance structure in the model and the adjustment is fully saturated:

fit_multishift <- ep_multi_shift(
  formula = cases ~ arm + age_grp,
  data = trial_design,
  offset = "person_years",
  offset_log = FALSE,
  exact_vars = "arm",
  ref_levels = list(arm = "placebo"),
  verbose = FALSE
)
fit_multishift$exactparmest
#>    Parameter Estimate StdError Alpha LowerCL    UpperCL  PValue SuffStat
#> 1 armvaccine     -Inf       NA  0.05    -Inf -0.1633296 0.03125        0
fit_network <- ep_network(
  formula = cases ~ arm + age_grp,
  data = trial_design,
  offset = "person_years",
  offset_log = FALSE,
  exact_vars = "arm",
  ref_levels = list(arm = "placebo"),
  verbose = FALSE
)
fit_network$exactparmest
#>    Parameter Estimate StdError Alpha LowerCL    UpperCL  PValue SuffStat
#> 1 armvaccine     -Inf       NA  0.05    -Inf -0.1633296 0.03125        0
all.equal(
  fit_exact$exactparmest[, c("Estimate", "LowerCL", "UpperCL", "PValue")],
  fit_multishift$exactparmest[, c("Estimate", "LowerCL", "UpperCL", "PValue")],
  tolerance = 1e-6
)
#> [1] TRUE
all.equal(
  fit_multishift$exactparmest[, c("Estimate", "LowerCL", "UpperCL", "PValue")],
  fit_network$exactparmest[, c("Estimate", "LowerCL", "UpperCL", "PValue")],
  tolerance = 1e-6
)
#> [1] TRUE

All three algorithms (the closed-form special case and both fully general algorithms) agree, exactly as vignette("Theory-Implementation") Sections 4 and 10.3 predict. This is a useful habit generally, not just for this example: running an unfamiliar model through more than one algorithm and comparing exactparmest is cheap insurance before relying on a result for anything important.

Reusing an already-computed exact distribution

Here is the part of this vignette that answers a different question: once ep_closed_form() has run, is every subsequent question about the same effect stuck re-running the whole enumeration?

vignette("Theory-Implementation") Section 6.5 derives the fact that makes the answer no: because the exponential-tilt family (3.3)/(6.3) sums to one at every value of \beta, a tail probability, and therefore a p-value against any null, or a confidence limit at any \alpha, can be recomputed directly from the already-built coefficient table, without rebuilding it. fit_exact$OUTDIST is that table:

parm <- "armvaccine"
dist1d <- fit_exact$OUTDIST[[parm]]
head(dist1d)
#>   SuffStat     prob LogWeight
#> 1        0 0.015625  0.000000
#> 2        1 0.093750  1.791759
#> 3        2 0.234375  2.708050
#> 4        3 0.312500  2.995732
#> 5        4 0.234375  2.708050
#> 6        5 0.093750  1.791759
t_obs <- fit_exact$exactparmest$SuffStat[
  fit_exact$exactparmest$Parameter == parm
]
t_obs
#> [1] 0

SuffStat is the attainable values of the sufficient statistic T (the vaccine-arm case count, summed over strata); LogWeight is \log C(t) (Section 3.4); prob is the null (\beta = 0) probability of each value, already normalized. Turning this table into a p-value or a confidence interval at a different null value or significance level is exactly what recompute_exact_inference() does: it is built from the same tilt-probability/root-finding machinery every fitting function already uses internally, exported as one small convenience wrapper, (see ?recompute_exact_inference).

A different null hypothesis: is efficacy above 50%, not just above 0%?

The original fit tested the usual null of no effect (\mathrm{RR}=1, \beta=0). A regulator might instead want to know whether this trial’s data are consistent with a pre-specified superiority margin, for example, whether the observed efficacy is significantly above 50%, i.e. H_0: \mathrm{RR}=0.50 against H_1: \mathrm{RR}<0.50 (equivalently, true VE exceeds 50%):

beta0_margin <- log(1 - 0.50) # beta corresponding to a 50% efficacy margin

margin_test <- recompute_exact_inference(fit_exact, parm, beta0 = beta0_margin)

cat(sprintf(
  "One-sided p-value for H0: VE = 50%% vs H1: VE > 50%%:  p = %.4f\n",
  margin_test$p_lower
))
#> One-sided p-value for H0: VE = 50% vs H1: VE > 50%:  p = 0.0878

Fewer vaccine-arm cases than the margin implies gives a small p_lower (evidence that true efficacy exceeds 50%); this is read directly off the lower tail of the same dist1d table used for the original test, evaluated at a different \beta_0: no new dynamic program, no new convolution, no new network pass.

A different confidence level: 90% instead of 95%

Likewise, a 90% interval instead of the original 95% one is a different \alpha applied to the same table:

ci_90 <- recompute_exact_inference(fit_exact, parm, alpha = 0.10)

rr_ci_90 <- exp(c(ci_90$LowerCL, ci_90$UpperCL))
ve_ci_90 <- rev(1 - rr_ci_90)

cat(sprintf(
  "90%% CI:  RR (%.3f, %.3f)   VE (%.1f%%, %.1f%%)\n",
  rr_ci_90[1],
  rr_ci_90[2],
  100 * ve_ci_90[1],
  100 * ve_ci_90[2]
))
#> 90% CI:  RR (0.000, 0.648)   VE (35.2%, 100.0%)

Both of these (a different null, and a different confidence level) are recomputed from fit_exact$OUTDIST alone. For this two-stratum-effect example the combinatorial work behind the original fit was already cheap, so the saving is mostly conceptual. But for a general model with several categorical covariates, run through ep_multi_shift() or ep_network(), building the joint coefficient table is exactly the expensive part (vignette("Theory-Implementation") Section 10); this is the part that answering a second question about the same effect never has to repeat.

A Monte Carlo check: does the nominal coverage actually hold?

Rather than rely on a single simulated trial to make the point, this section repeats the simulation many times and refits both ways each time. Every replicate is kept, including every all-zero-vaccine-arm replicate (roughly a 1-in-8 chance each time, e^{-2.1} \approx 0.122), because the point of this section is to measure what actually happens across the full range of outcomes this design can produce, boundary cases included, rather than to report a tidy number that only describes the well-behaved fits.

Two things make a plain confidence-interval-width comparison a poor fit for that goal here. First, a replicate at the boundary gives the exact method an -Inf lower limit, which forces any width computed from it to be Inf; averaging widths across replicates that include even one such case is not informative. Second, and more importantly, glm()’s own $converged flag and its warnings are both supposed to be the tools for catching a bad fit, and the single worked example above already showed both can stay silent. So instead of interval width, this simulation tracks the diagnostics a user would actually have available: whether each method’s interval excludes the null in the correct direction (statistical significance for a genuine vaccine effect), whether glm() itself reports having converged, and whether its standard error is a plausible number at all.

n_sims <- 1000
set.seed(20260731)

# On the beta (log rate ratio) scale, a well-behaved fit in this design never
# produces a standard error above about 1.5; a fit that has hit the all-zero
# vaccine-arm boundary produces one in the tens of thousands (see the single
# worked example earlier in this vignette). A threshold of 10 sits with a
# wide safety margin between the two and cleanly separates them.
se_large_cutoff <- 10

one_rep <- function() {
  d <- trial_design
  d$cases <- rpois(nrow(d), d$expected_cases)

  fit_i <- ep_closed_form(
    cases ~ arm,
    data = d,
    offset = "person_years",
    offset_log = FALSE,
    strata = "age_grp",
    ref_levels = list(arm = "placebo"),
    verbose = FALSE
  )
  exact_row <- fit_i$exactparmest
  exact_covers <- (exact_row$LowerCL <= true_beta) &&
    (true_beta <= exact_row$UpperCL)
  # "Significant" here means the entire CI for beta sits below 0, i.e., the
  # rate ratio's CI sits below 1, i.e., the VE% CI's lower limit sits above 0%.
  exact_sig <- exact_row$UpperCL < 0

  ws <- character(0)
  glm_i <- withCallingHandlers(
    glm(
      cases ~ arm + age_grp + offset(log(person_years)),
      family = poisson,
      data = d
    ),
    warning = function(w) {
      ws <<- c(ws, conditionMessage(w))
      invokeRestart("muffleWarning")
    }
  )
  co_i <- summary(glm_i)$coefficients["armvaccine", ]
  se_i <- co_i["Std. Error"]
  lo_i <- co_i["Estimate"] - z975 * se_i
  hi_i <- co_i["Estimate"] + z975 * se_i
  wald_covers <- (lo_i <= true_beta) && (true_beta <= hi_i)
  wald_sig <- hi_i < 0

  data.frame(
    exact_covers = exact_covers,
    exact_sig = exact_sig,
    wald_covers = wald_covers,
    wald_sig = wald_sig,
    glm_not_converged = !isTRUE(glm_i$converged),
    se_large = se_i > se_large_cutoff,
    glm_flagged = length(ws) > 0
  )
}

mc_results <- do.call(rbind, lapply(seq_len(n_sims), function(i) one_rep()))

mc_summary <- data.frame(
  Method = c("Exact (closed-form)", "Wald (glm)"),
  `Nominal level` = "95%",
  `Empirical coverage` = c(
    mean(mc_results$exact_covers),
    mean(mc_results$wald_covers)
  ),
  `% VE significant` = c(
    100 * mean(mc_results$exact_sig),
    100 * mean(mc_results$wald_sig)
  ),
  `% glm() did not converge` = c(NA, 100 * mean(mc_results$glm_not_converged)),
  `% SE very large` = c(NA, 100 * mean(mc_results$se_large)),
  `% glm() flagged a warning` = c(NA, 100 * mean(mc_results$glm_flagged)),
  check.names = FALSE
)
knitr::kable(mc_summary, digits = 3)
Method Nominal level Empirical coverage % VE significant % glm() did not converge % SE very large % glm() flagged a warning
Exact (closed-form) 95% 0.983 25.5 NA NA NA
Wald (glm) 95% 0.968 17.0 0 12.5 3.3

Every replicate is included in every column above, boundary and non-boundary alike, so this table is a direct empirical answer to “what actually happens across 1000 trials of this size,” not a description of only the trials that happened to behave nicely.

% glm() did not converge is 0.0%. glm()’s own convergence flag never once reports a problem in this experiment, including on every replicate where the vaccine arm came back with zero events. Checking $converged is not a safety net here: it is uniformly, uninformatively TRUE.

% SE very large is 12.5%, and this is not a coincidence: it matches the all-zero-vaccine-arm boundary rate almost exactly, because that boundary is precisely what drives the standard error to an implausible size in this design. Unlike $converged, a standard error of the estimate’s own magnitude is at least, in principle, something a careful user could notice; the trouble, as the single worked example demonstrated, is that nothing in glm()’s default output forces that noticing to happen.

% glm() flagged a warning is only 3.3%, far short of the 12.5% of replicates that actually have a blown-up standard error. Most of the replicates driving that 12.5% figure produce no diagnostic message whatsoever; the warning some replicates do trigger (glm.fit: fitted rates numerically 0 occurred) depends on the fitted rate underflowing to exact floating-point zero, which happens on some but not all of the boundary replicates, essentially by numerical accident.

% VE significant is where the practical cost of this shows up most directly: the exact method flags a significant vaccine effect on 25.5% of replicates, against only 17.0% for the Wald method, even though both are analysing the identical simulated data every time. The gap is concentrated exactly among the boundary replicates: with zero vaccine-arm events, the exact method’s UpperCL is still a small, finite, sub-zero number (as the single worked example showed, UpperCL \approx -0.16, correctly significant), while the Wald method’s own hi_i is a huge positive number on those same replicates, so it never registers as significant at all. glm() does not merely produce an uninformative interval on a boundary replicate; it actively loses the power to detect a real effect exactly where the data are sparsest, which is exactly where a trial’s analysis plan needs that power the most.

A more general model: adjusting for a covariate on top of stratification

Every fit so far has used age_grp purely as strata, the one special case ep_closed_form() handles, where strata are the only nuisance structure in the model (vignette("Theory-Implementation") Section 6.1). Real studies often need more than that: an ordinary categorical covariate to adjust for, in addition to stratification, that is not itself under test. Suppose this trial had also recorded each participant’s baseline risk status (risk_group: "standard" or "high"), a real confounder (high-risk participants have a higher baseline incidence rate regardless of arm or age) that the analysis should adjust for without testing it. That is exactly the model ep_closed_form() cannot fit (it only accepts a single two-level effect, with strata as the sole other structure); this is what ep_multi_shift() and ep_network() are for.

set.seed(20260819)

design_adj <- expand.grid(
  age_grp = age_grp,
  arm = c("placebo", "vaccine"),
  risk_group = factor(c("standard", "high"), levels = c("standard", "high")),
  KEEP.OUT.ATTRS = FALSE
)
design_adj$arm <- factor(design_adj$arm, levels = c("placebo", "vaccine"))

placebo_rate_by_age <- c(
  "18-40" = 0.0060,
  "41-64" = 0.0100,
  "65+"   = 0.0180
)
person_years_by_age <- c(
  "18-40" = 2000,
  "41-64" = 1500,
  "65+"   = 500
)
risk_mult  <- c(standard = 1.0, high = 1.6)
risk_share <- c(standard = 0.65, high = 0.35)

design_adj$placebo_rate <-
  placebo_rate_by_age[as.character(design_adj$age_grp)]
design_adj$person_years <-
  person_years_by_age[as.character(design_adj$age_grp)] *
  risk_share[as.character(design_adj$risk_group)]
design_adj$true_rate <- with(
  design_adj,
  placebo_rate * risk_mult[as.character(risk_group)] *
    ifelse(arm == "vaccine", true_rr, 1)
)
design_adj$expected_cases <- design_adj$person_years * design_adj$true_rate
design_adj$cases <- rpois(nrow(design_adj), design_adj$expected_cases)

design_adj[, c(
  "age_grp",
  "arm",
  "risk_group",
  "person_years",
  "expected_cases",
  "cases"
)]
#>    age_grp     arm risk_group person_years expected_cases cases
#> 1    18-40 placebo   standard         1300          7.800     9
#> 2    41-64 placebo   standard          975          9.750     6
#> 3      65+ placebo   standard          325          5.850     7
#> 4    18-40 vaccine   standard         1300          2.340     3
#> 5    41-64 vaccine   standard          975          2.925     1
#> 6      65+ vaccine   standard          325          1.755     0
#> 7    18-40 placebo       high          700          6.720     7
#> 8    41-64 placebo       high          525          8.400     4
#> 9      65+ placebo       high          175          5.040     3
#> 10   18-40 vaccine       high          700          2.016     0
#> 11   41-64 vaccine       high          525          2.520     3
#> 12     65+ vaccine       high          175          1.512     1

The vaccine effect (arm) is still constant across every stratum and every risk group, by construction (true VE = 70%, exactly as before); only the baseline rate differs by risk_group, which is exactly what “adjusting for a confounder” means: something that shifts everyone’s baseline risk without itself being the effect of interest, and without modifying how strongly arm acts. exact_vars = "arm" tests only the vaccine effect; risk_group enters formula like any other covariate and is conditioned on (by default, condition_on = "model") rather than tested:

fit_adj <- ep_multi_shift(
  formula = cases ~ arm + risk_group,
  data = design_adj,
  offset = "person_years",
  offset_log = FALSE,
  strata = "age_grp",
  exact_vars = "arm",
  ref_levels = list(arm = "placebo", risk_group = "standard"),
  verbose = FALSE
)
fit_adj$exactparmest
#>    Parameter  Estimate StdError Alpha   LowerCL    UpperCL      PValue SuffStat
#> 1 armvaccine -1.504077 0.390868  0.05 -2.416557 -0.7211634 2.54486e-05        8
rr_adj <- exp(fit_adj$exactparmest$Estimate)
rr_ci_adj <- exp(c(fit_adj$exactparmest$LowerCL, fit_adj$exactparmest$UpperCL))
ve_adj <- 1 - rr_adj
ve_ci_adj <- rev(1 - rr_ci_adj)

cat(sprintf(
  paste("Exact (adjusted for risk_group): RR = %.3f (95%% CI %.3f, %.3f)",
   "  VE = %.1f%% (95%% CI %.1f%%, %.1f%%)   p = %.4f\n"),
  rr_adj,
  rr_ci_adj[1],
  rr_ci_adj[2],
  100 * ve_adj,
  100 * ve_ci_adj[1],
  100 * ve_ci_adj[2],
  fit_adj$exactparmest$PValue
))
#> Exact (adjusted for risk_group): RR = 0.222 (95% CI 0.089, 0.486)   VE = 77.8% (95% CI 51.4%, 91.1%)   p = 0.0000

As in every other example in this vignette, ep_network() must agree exactly with ep_multi_shift() on this same model: both algorithms answer the identical question, just by different computational routes (vignette("Theory-Implementation") Sections 4 and 10.3):

fit_adj_net <- ep_network(
  formula = cases ~ arm + risk_group,
  data = design_adj,
  offset = "person_years",
  offset_log = FALSE,
  strata = "age_grp",
  exact_vars = "arm",
  ref_levels = list(arm = "placebo", risk_group = "standard"),
  verbose = FALSE
)
all.equal(
  fit_adj$exactparmest[, c("Estimate", "LowerCL", "UpperCL", "PValue")],
  fit_adj_net$exactparmest[, c("Estimate", "LowerCL", "UpperCL", "PValue")]
)
#> [1] TRUE

For comparison, the asymptotic glm() fit of the identical model (arm, age_grp, and risk_group all as ordinary covariates, exactly the same saturation argument vignette("Theory-Implementation") Section 4.1-4.2 makes for strata alone):

glm_adj <- glm(
  cases ~ arm + age_grp + risk_group + offset(log(person_years)),
  family = poisson(link = "log"),
  data = design_adj
)
summary(glm_adj)$coefficients
#>                   Estimate Std. Error      z value     Pr(>|z|)
#> (Intercept)    -4.95244436  0.2709545 -18.27777443 1.243997e-74
#> armvaccine     -1.50407740  0.3908673  -3.84805136 1.190611e-04
#> age_grp41-64   -0.01769958  0.3522216  -0.05025125 9.599222e-01
#> age_grp65+      0.83975065  0.3788675   2.21647606 2.665892e-02
#> risk_grouphigh  0.25131443  0.3066219   0.81962309 4.124310e-01

Finally, note what happens if ep_closed_form() is asked to fit this same model: it refuses, rather than silently ignoring risk_group and returning an unadjusted (and therefore biased) estimate:

ep_closed_form(
  formula = cases ~ arm + risk_group,
  data = design_adj,
  offset = "person_years",
  offset_log = FALSE,
  strata = "age_grp",
  ref_levels = list(arm = "placebo", risk_group = "standard"),
  verbose = FALSE
)
#> Error:
#> ! `formula` must contain exactly one right-hand-side term (the
#>                 effect to test), with strata and the offset supplied separately
#>                 via the `strata`/`offset` arguments, not as additional terms in
#>                 `formula`; found term(s): arm, risk_group. Use `ep_multi_shift()` or
#>                 `ep_network()` for models with additional categorical
#>                 covariates.

That error message is the package telling you which function to use: any time there’s more structure to condition on than strata alone, ep_closed_form() is the wrong tool, and ep_multi_shift()/ep_network() are what this vignette’s earlier sections on reusing an already-built distribution and recomputing inference at a different null/alpha apply to just as well.

References

  • See vignette("Theory-Implementation") for the full derivation of every method used here, and for the complete reference list (Guess, Lydick, Small and Miller 1987; Guess and Thomas 1990; Hirji, Mehta and Patel 1987; Mehta, Patel and Senchaudhuri 1992; and others).
  • ICH E9(R1), Addendum on Estimands and Sensitivity Analysis in Clinical Trials, for the convention (used in vignette("Theory-Implementation") Section 4.7 and followed here) of carrying a trial’s randomization-stratification factors into the primary analysis as strata.
